title: Meet the Brain
subtitle: One organ, many coordinated systems
learningObjectives: Describe the brain as interacting cortical, subcortical, cerebellar and brainstem systems.
Explain why connectivity is as clinically important as regional specialisation.
Use regional activation cautiously and avoid reverse inference.

sections.explainSimply: The brain is a team of regions that share information. No single area works completely alone.
sections.explainLikePsychologist: Functions emerge from distributed networks spanning cortex, subcortex, cerebellum and brainstem. Regional specialisation matters, but connectivity determines performance.
sections.advancedClinicalDetail: Large-scale networks dynamically reconfigure according to task demands, arousal and learning. Structure–function relationships are probabilistic, not one-to-one mappings.
sections.thinkOfItLike: An orchestra: sections specialise, but the music depends on timing, coordination and the conductor’s changing demands.
sections.whyPsychologistsCare: Avoid reverse inference—observing activation in a region does not prove a specific thought, diagnosis or emotion.
sections.whenItGoesWrong: Focal lesions can disrupt specialised functions, while diffuse or connectivity disturbances may produce broader cognitive and emotional effects.
sections.clinicalPearl: Think in systems first, regions second, and isolated “brain centres” last.
sections.practicalExample: A patient with a focal lesion may show deficits beyond the damaged tissue because connected network nodes lose input or alter their activity. Behaviour therefore reflects both local damage and network consequences.
sections.limitationsCautions: Functional labels are probabilistic summaries. Individual organisation varies with development, experience, pathology and task demands, and neuroimaging activation is not equivalent to a diagnosis.

quizBank.question: Which statement best reflects modern neuroscience?
options: Each emotion has one brain centre
quizBank.explanation: Most psychological functions rely on coordinated activity across distributed, interacting networks.
